records.name: House of Liechtenstein (Princely Family; LGT Group)
records.scaleNote: No documented role in the Atlantic slave trade was found. The profile is included because of the family's very large present-day wealth: LGT, the bank it owns, reported CHF 386.1bn in client assets under management at end-2025.
records.origins: An Austrian noble family that rose in Habsburg service and was raised to princely rank in 1608. It bought the lordships of Schellenberg and Vaduz, which became the Principality of Liechtenstein in 1719. Most of its wealth lay in large estates in Bohemia and Moravia until Czechoslovakia confiscated them in 1945.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in the Atlantic slave trade or in colonial slavery. This record exists to answer the 'hidden old wealth' question: the family's fortune came from Central European land, Habsburg court office and, since the 1930s, private banking.

roleDetail.d: Until 1945 the family's core assets were estates in the Bohemian lands, worked under the serf labour system until 1848. That was a European system of unfree labour, not the Atlantic trade.

Searches for a Liechtenstein chartered company, plantation holdings or slave-trade investment found none. The Liechtenstein–Czech Historians' Commission's work deals with the Bohemian and Moravian estates, not with colonies.

records.legacy: The family wholly owns LGT, one of Europe's largest family-owned private banks, and holds a major art collection displayed at the Liechtenstein palaces in Vienna. Hans-Adam II is regularly ranked Europe's richest monarch.

legacyDetail.d: Per LGT's 2025 results, group profit was CHF 445.6m and assets under management CHF 386.1bn. The family has controlled the bank for over 90 years.

Their wealth sits mainly in LGT, family foundations, Austrian and Liechtenstein property, and the princely collections.

records.name: Thurn und Taxis family (Princes of Thurn und Taxis)
records.scaleNote: No documented role in the slave trade. The fortune came from the hereditary Imperial postal monopoly (c. 1490s–1867) and later from land, forests and brewing.
records.origins: A courier family from Cornello near Bergamo. Franz von Taxis ran the Habsburg courier network between Innsbruck and Brussels from the 1490s. In 1615 Emperor Matthias made the office of Imperial Postmaster General a hereditary fief of the family.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in slavery or the slave trade. The family ran Europe's main postal network for the Habsburgs and the Holy Roman Empire. That was a service to the same crowns that licensed the trade, but no tie to the trade itself was found.

roleDetail.d: The Imperial Post (Kaiserliche Reichspost) was run by the family from c. 1600 to 1806. The Thurn-und-Taxis Post continued until it was sold to Prussia in 1867.
The family's own history and standard references mention no colonies, plantations, Atlantic shipping or slave-trade investment.

records.legacy: The family remains one of Germany's largest private landowners, with nearly 20,000 hectares of forest (Euronews, 2026). Its seat is the former abbey of St Emmeram in Regensburg. After Prince Johannes died in 1990, Princess Gloria sold assets to settle large debts and inheritance tax.

legacyDetail.t: Largest private forest owner in Germany.
legacyDetail.d: Euronews (2026) gives 'knapp 20,000 hectares'. The family sold more than 5,000 hectares in 2004.

records.name: House of Hesse (Hesse-Kassel line; Landgraves and Electors of Hesse)
records.scaleNote: Hesse-Kassel sent c. 17,000 soldiers to fight for Britain in North America (1776–83) under subsidy treaties. It had no documented role in the slave trade or in plantations.
records.origins: The Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel financed their state partly by hiring out their army to foreign powers. In January 1776 Landgrave Frederick II agreed to supply Britain with 12,000 soldiers. Later about a quarter of Britain's land forces in America were German auxiliaries, called 'Hessians'.
records.role_summary: The house hired out soldiers to Britain, and they fought to hold slaveholding colonies. In March 1779 France protested that Hessians were fighting in the Antilles, and the Landgrave replied that the Antilles 'belonged to' North America. Historian Friederike Baer finds no evidence that Hessian regiments were actually sent to the West Indies. Hessian units took in formerly enslaved Black men, some recruited and some captured, mostly as drummers. About 100 or more went back with the troops to Kassel.

roleDetail.d: Under the 15 January 1776 treaty Hesse-Kassel supplied 12,000 men. Some 16,992 Hesse-Kassel soldiers served in North America.
The 1779 French complaint about Hessians in the Antilles (possibly St Lucia, 1778) is documented. Baer notes that no German regiment was in the St Lucia expedition and that the question remains open.
Hessian regiments enlisted or seized formerly enslaved African Americans, mostly as drummers. Roughly 100–200 Black men, women and children went to Germany with the troops (Musgrave; Hoffman 1981).

Mayer Amschel Rothschild became a court agent to the future William IX/I in 1769. He handled British payments for hired Hessian troops and, from 1806, hid the Elector's fortune from Napoleon. That business launched the Rothschild bank.

records.legacy: The Elector's fortune, swollen by British subsidies, was the seed capital of the Rothschild network. Today the Hessische Hausstiftung (House of Hesse Foundation) owns palaces, art and hotels. In January 2026 Landgrave Donatus offered its cultural foundation to the State of Hesse.

legacyDetail.d: Hessenschau (27 Jan 2026), citing the FAZ, reported an internal valuation of c. €450m for the properties and art. Schloss Friedrichshof (Kronberg) and Schloss Fasanerie are among the properties offered.

records.name: House of Hohenzollern (Brandenburg-Prussia; Sigmaringen line)
records.scaleNote: Historians estimate the Brandenburg African Company, chartered by the Hohenzollern Great Elector, shipped up to c. 20,000 Africans in 1680–1717, about one in ten dying at sea (Postcolonial Potsdam).
records.base: Berlin and Potsdam (Prussian line); Sigmaringen (Swabian line)
records.origins: Margraves and Electors of Brandenburg from 1415, Kings in/of Prussia from 1701, German Emperors 1871–1918. A separate Catholic Swabian line (Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen) kept its estates in south-west Germany.
records.role_summary: Elector Frederick William (the Great Elector) backed Raule's 1680–81 Guinea expedition, chartered the Brandenburg African Company in 1682 and built Groß Friedrichsburg on the Gold Coast. The company bought captives and sold them in the Caribbean from a leased base on Danish St Thomas. His grandson King Frederick William I sold the forts to the Dutch WIC in 1717 (transfer completed c. 1720–21) for c. 7,000–7,200 ducats and 12 enslaved Africans.

roleDetail.d: The details are in the existing records frederick-william-brandenburg and brandenburg-african-company. The dynasty owned the venture, so this tie is documented.
Raule was commissioned to bring young Africans to serve at the Elector's court.
The Prussian line descends from the Great Elector. The Sigmaringen line is a distant Swabian branch with no tie to the African company.

records.legacy: Groß Friedrichsburg survives at Princes Town, Ghana. In 2025 the Prussian line settled a near-century-old dispute with the German state: c. 3,000 objects went into a new public Hohenzollern Art Collection Foundation, with a 6:3 public-to-family board.

legacyDetail.d: The Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation's board approved the agreement on 26 May 2025. The family keeps some 'C-list' items.

records.name: House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha (Belgian, British and Portuguese lines)
records.scaleNote: No role in the Atlantic slave trade was found. The family came to its thrones after Britain's 1807 and 1833 abolition acts. Its gravest record is Leopold II's Congo Free State (1885–1908), a later colonial forced-labour regime, not the Atlantic trade.
records.origins: A small Thuringian ducal house that placed Leopold I on the Belgian throne (1831), Ferdinand as king consort of Portugal (1836) and Prince Albert as Queen Victoria's consort (1840). The British royal house bore the name from Edward VII (1901) until it was renamed Windsor in 1917.
records.role_summary: Atlantic slave trade: no documented involvement. Belgian line: Leopold II personally owned the Congo Free State (1885–1908). He ran it through a regime of forced rubber and ivory collection enforced by the Force Publique, with mass violence and a population collapse; estimates range widely and are debated, with disease a major cause. This was colonial forced labour after the era of the Atlantic trade, run in the name of 'anti-slavery'. Portuguese line: its kings reigned while slavery lasted in Portugal's African colonies until the 1869 decree and the end of 'liberto' status (1876–78).

roleDetail.t: Congo Free State (forced labour, not the Atlantic trade).
roleDetail.d: Leopold II's profits from forced labour helped fund the 1900 Royal Donation (Royal Trust) of palaces and land still at the Belgian royal family's disposal.

roleDetail.t: British line inherits earlier crown ties.
roleDetail.d: The British monarchy's slave-trade links come from the Stuart and Hanoverian crowns (RAC, South Sea Company). In 2023 the Guardian found a 1689 RAC share transfer to William III. Charles III backed independent research into these links (Camilla de Koning, Manchester; co-sponsored by Historic Royal Palaces).

Ferdinand II (king consort 1837–53) and his sons Pedro V and Luís I reigned while slavery continued in Portuguese Africa. The 25 February 1869 decree abolished it, turning enslaved people into 'libertos' bound to work until 1876–78.

records.legacy: On 30 June 2020 King Philippe wrote to President Tshisekedi expressing his 'deepest regrets' for 'acts of violence and cruelty' in the Congo. It was not a formal apology. The Royal Trust, partly funded by Congo profits, holds c. 7,500 ha and 77 buildings, valued at at least €231.4m in its first disclosure (Belga).

legacyDetail.d: Created from Leopold II's 1900 donation, it was enlarged when he ceded the Congo to Belgium in 1908. Its properties cannot be sold and stay at the royal family's disposal.
Buckingham Palace said in April 2023 that the King takes the issue 'profoundly seriously' and opened the Royal Archives to the PhD project.

records.name: House of Habsburg (Spanish and Austrian lines; Habsburg-Lorraine)
records.scaleNote: As kings of Castile and Aragon (1516–1700), the Spanish Habsburgs licensed the transatlantic trade to Spanish America: the 1518 licence for 4,000 Africans, the Portuguese asientos from 1595 (Reinel) to 1640, and the Grillo-Lomellini asiento of 1662.
records.origins: A Swabian-Swiss comital family that became Holy Roman Emperors. Through Charles V (r. Spain 1516–56) it inherited Castile, Aragon and the Indies. The Spanish line ruled until 1700. The Austrian line, descended from Charles V's brother Ferdinand I, continued as Habsburg-Lorraine.
records.role_summary: Spanish Habsburg kings turned the slave trade into a crown revenue system. Charles V's 1518 licence to Gorrevod opened direct Africa–America shipments. Philip II and his successors sold monopoly asientos (Reinel 1595; Portuguese contractors to 1640; Grillo and Lomellini 1662). Charles V also granted Venezuela to the Welser. The crown institution is in crown-of-castile; this record is the dynasty.

roleDetail.d: See charter-1518, spanish-asiento, pedro-gomes-reinel and grillo-and-lomellini. All were issued by Habsburg kings.

roleDetail.t: Financed by the Fugger, Welser and Genoese.
roleDetail.d: The crown's loans from the Augsburg and Genoese houses were tied to the same royal finances that sold slave-trade licences.
The surviving Habsburg-Lorraine line descends from Ferdinand I, not from the Spanish kings who issued the asientos. No separate Austrian Habsburg slave-trade role was found.

records.legacy: Austria's 1919 Habsburg Law transferred court and entailed family-fund assets to the Republic. The law is still in constitutional force and is confirmed by the 1955 State Treaty. The family kept 'considerable private' assets, but repeated restitution claims have failed.

legacyDetail.d: Austrian arbitration panels (2004) rejected family claims because constitutional law and the State Treaty bar restitution.

records.name: House of Bourbon (French, Spanish and Orléans lines)
records.scaleNote: French Bourbon kings chartered the slave-trading companies and issued the Code Noir (1685). Philip V gave the 1701 asiento to the Compagnie de Guinée and in 1713 ceded it to Britain's South Sea Company. Charles IV's 1789 decree opened free trade in captives to Spanish America, fuelling Cuba's slave-trade boom.
records.origins: A Capetian cadet line that took the French throne with Henri IV (1589). Louis XIV's grandson Philip V founded the Spanish Bourbons in 1700. The Orléans and Two Sicilies lines are further branches. The French crown institution is the existing record crown-of-france.
records.role_summary: In France the Bourbons chartered the Compagnie des Indes, Sénégal and Guinée companies, issued the Code Noir (1685) and, under Charles X, imposed the 1825 indemnity on Haiti. In Spain Philip V moved the asiento from the Habsburg system to the French Compagnie de Guinée (1701) and then to Britain (Utrecht, 1713). Charles IV liberalised the trade (1789). Ferdinand VII signed the 1817 treaty with Britain to end it, but the trade to Cuba continued illegally. According to historian Martín Rodrigo, Queen Regent María Cristina and her husband Agustín Fernando Muñoz were among those who profited from the illegal Cuban trade.

roleDetail.t: Code Noir and the French companies.
roleDetail.d: See code-noir, compagnie-de-guinee and crown-of-france.
Philip V granted the asiento to the Compagnie de Guinée (1701). The Treaty of Utrecht transferred it to the South Sea Company (1713).
Charles IV's royal cédula of February 1789 let Spanish subjects and foreigners trade captives freely into Cuba, Santo Domingo, Puerto Rico and Caracas.

roleDetail.t: María Cristina and the illegal Cuban trade.
roleDetail.d: The Barcelona Maritime Museum's 2025 exhibition, advised by Martín Rodrigo, names her and Muñoz among the trade's profiteers. Detailed archival proof was not reviewed here.

records.legacy: Spanish Bourbons reign today (Felipe VI). The French claimants are Louis Alphonse, Duke of Anjou (Legitimist) and Jean, Count of Paris (Orléanist). Île Bourbon (Réunion), Bourbon Street (New Orleans) and Bourbon County (Kentucky) carry the name.

legacyDetail.d: In April 2022 the Royal Household published his assets as €2,573,392 (savings, securities, art, jewellery), with no property. In 2020 he renounced any inheritance from Juan Carlos.

records.name: House of Wittelsbach (Dukes, Electors and Kings of Bavaria)
records.scaleNote: No documented role in the Atlantic slave trade was found for the Bavarian line. A collateral branch (Palatinate-Zweibrücken) gave Sweden three kings (1654–1718) during and after the Swedish Africa Company's short Gold Coast venture.
records.origins: Rulers of Bavaria from 1180 to 1918, with branches in the Palatinate, Sweden (Charles X Gustav, Charles XI, Charles XII) and Greece (Otto). After 1918 a 1923 agreement with the Free State of Bavaria created the Wittelsbacher Ausgleichsfonds (WAF) to support the family.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in slavery or the slave trade for the Bavarian line. The Swedish Gold Coast post Carolusborg (1653) is often said to be named after Charles X Gustav of the Palatinate-Zweibrücken branch. The company was chartered under Queen Christina (Vasa) and lost its forts by 1663. That is a cousin branch's crown office, too remote to count as a tie for the Bavarian house.

roleDetail.d: Charles X Gustav reigned 1654–60, as the Swedish Africa Company traded on the Gold Coast (1650–63). The Swedish slave trade in that period was small.
The fund was created on 9 March 1923 to settle the family's claims after the monarchy ended.

records.legacy: The WAF holds c. 12,000 ha of forest, Berg and Grünau castles, central Munich property and the Hirschgarten beer garden, and lends c. 43,000 cultural objects to state museums. Family line heads receive c. €14m a year. The Bavarian Court of Audit does not audit it.

legacyDetail.d: The Finance Ministry gave the WAF's value as €348m (2016) and €444m (2018), excluding art.

records.name: House of Grimaldi (Princes of Monaco)
records.scaleNote: No documented slave-trade involvement was found for the Monaco line. The wider Genoese Grimaldi clan traded between Seville and Hispaniola (1489–1517), but the study of that network found here does not document dealing in captives.
records.origins: A Genoese patrician family that seized Monaco in 1297. The male line died out in 1731, and the house continued through Louise-Hippolyte Grimaldi's marriage to Jacques de Goyon de Matignon, who took the Grimaldi name. The Genoese Grimaldi 'albergo' was a wider clan of merchants and bankers, distinct from the Monaco princes.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement of the Monaco princes in slavery or the slave trade. Genoese merchants (Centurione, Grillo, Lomellini and others) were central to early Spanish slave licences and asientos, and Grimaldi merchants such as Jerónimo Grimaldi ran a Seville–Santo Domingo trading house in 1489–1517. A slave-trade role for them is not shown in the sources found, and they were not the Monaco line.

roleDetail.d: The Genoese buyers of Gorrevod's 1518 licence and the 1662 Grillo-Lomellini asiento are documented. No Grimaldi is named among them in the sources checked.
Searches for Grimaldi or Matignon property in Saint-Domingue or other French slave colonies found nothing.

records.legacy: The princely family reigns over Monaco. The Société des Bains de Mer (casinos and hotels) is majority state-owned. Albert II's personal fortune has been estimated at about US$1bn.

legacyDetail.d: Forbes put Albert II at c. US$1bn in 2011 (reported by the Sunday Times, South Africa).

records.name: Wallenberg family (Investor AB, SEB)
records.scaleNote: No documented role in slavery. The family bank, Stockholms Enskilda Bank, was founded in 1856, nine years after Sweden ended slavery on Saint-Barthélemy (1847).
records.origins: André Oscar Wallenberg (1816–1886), a naval officer and son of the Bishop of Linköping, founded Stockholms Enskilda Bank in 1856. It merged in 1972 into SEB. The family's industrial holdings are pooled in Investor AB, whose largest owner has been the Wallenberg Foundations since 1917.
records.role_summary: No documented involvement in slavery or the slave trade. The Swedish Caribbean colony of Saint-Barthélemy (1784–1878) and its slave trade predate the Wallenberg bank. No Wallenberg ties to it were found. The family's historical controversies are elsewhere, notably its Second World War dealings with Germany.

roleDetail.t: Timing rules out St Barth slavery.
roleDetail.d: Slavery on St Barthélemy ended on 9 October 1847, when the Swedish state bought the freedom of the last 523 enslaved people. Enskilda Bank opened in 1856.

records.legacy: Investor AB reported adjusted net asset value of SEK 1,087.1bn at end-2025. Its holdings include ABB, Atlas Copco, Ericsson, AstraZeneca, SEB and Saab. Investor paid SEK 3.7bn to the Wallenberg Foundations in 2025, and the foundations mainly fund Swedish research.

legacyDetail.d: The family controls rather than owns most of the fortune, through the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation and sister foundations.

records.name: House of Bernadotte (Swedish royal family)
records.scaleNote: Bernadotte kings ruled Sweden's slaveholding Caribbean colony of Saint-Barthélemy from 1818 until abolition in 1847, when the state bought the freedom of the last 523 enslaved people. The island traded captives illegally into the 1830s (Uppsala University).
records.origins: French marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte was elected Swedish crown prince in 1810 and reigned as Karl XIV Johan (1818–44). Sweden had acquired Saint-Barthélemy from France in 1784 under Gustav III (House of Holstein-Gottorp, not Bernadotte).
records.role_summary: Karl XIV Johan governed the colony closely from 1810 to 1844 and sought more colonies (Uppsala University). Saint-Barthélemy was a free port where enslaved people were bought and sold illegally, including onward to Cuba, despite Sweden's 1813–15 treaty commitments. Under Oscar I the state abolished slavery there and bought the last 523 enslaved people free on 9 October 1847.

roleDetail.d: The colony was a crown possession. Earlier Swedish kings had set slave-trade rules (royal letter 1786; 1790 tax on shipments of West Africans).
Uppsala's ERC-funded project (Fredrik Thomasson) documents the island as a market for illegal captives. In 1809 one ship landed 378 Africans.
In 1847 the Swedish state bought out the owners of the last enslaved people.

records.legacy: Sweden sold Saint-Barthélemy back to France in 1878. Uppsala University now leads major research on Swedish Caribbean slavery, and Saint-Barthélemy will be named on the Paris slavery memorial. No royal statement on the colony was found.

legacyDetail.d: Fredrik Thomasson's ERC project (2024–28) studies Swedish participation in Caribbean slavery and colonialism.

records.name: Imperial House of Brazil (Braganza and Orléans-Braganza)
records.scaleNote: The Brazilian Empire (1822–89) was the largest importer of enslaved Africans in its era. More than 500,000 were brought in illegally after the 1831 ban, until the 1850 Eusébio de Queirós law (IHU Unisinos estimate). The crown estate of Santa Cruz was worked by enslaved people.
records.origins: A branch of Portugal's Braganza dynasty (crown-of-portugal) that founded the Brazilian Empire under Pedro I (1822). The present house descends from Princess Isabel, daughter of Pedro II, and her husband Gaston d'Orléans, Count of Eu, hence 'Orléans-Braganza'.
records.role_summary: The emperors reigned over a slave society. Pedro I's government passed the 1831 ban but did not enforce it, so imports continued on a vast scale until 1850. The royal and imperial Santa Cruz estate near Rio was worked by enslaved people; a manuscript of 1820 records 'slaves of the Brazilian Royal Family' there. Princess Isabel, as regent, signed the Lei Áurea on 13 May 1888, abolishing slavery without compensation. The monarchy fell in 1889.

roleDetail.d: Vanderbilt holds an 1820 table of births, deaths and escapes of enslaved people at the royal Santa Cruz plantation. A Fiocruz thesis studies its enslaved community under the Empire.
The 1831 Feijó law was 'a law for the English to see'. People imported illegally after 1831 were not freed by the 1850 law.
The Lei Áurea (1888) was signed by Princess Isabel; see lei-aurea-1888.

records.legacy: The Petrópolis branch still collects the 'laudêmio', a 2.5% charge on property sales in the area of Pedro I's former imperial farm (bought from 1830). It is paid to the Companhia Imobiliária de Petrópolis, which reported revenue of R$5.16m in 2020. The fee drew criticism after the 2022 Petrópolis floods.

legacyDetail.d: The Vassouras branch (Dom Bertrand) says it receives none of the laudêmio. Its father sold his share in the 1940s.

records.description: Caribbean island acquired by Gustav III from France in 1784. records.name: Congo Free State (1885–1908)
records.description: Territory held personally by Leopold II of Belgium from 1885 until Belgium annexed it on 15 November 1908. Rubber and ivory were extracted through forced labour enforced by the Force Publique, with killings, hostage-taking and village burnings. Estimates of population decline range from c. 1 to 10+ million and are debated, with disease a major cause. This was colonial forced labour after the Atlantic slave trade, presented by Leopold as an 'anti-slavery' mission. Its profits partly endowed the Belgian Royal Trust.
